children: When a top fund manager who can buy any kind of bond is cutting way back on corporates, investors ought to pay attention.

"We have the least amount of corporate credit risk the strategy has ever had," says Daniel Ivascyn, manager of the $223 billion Pimco Income fund, who finds the yields and risks of corporate bonds unattractive.

Pimco Income isn't just the largest multisector bond fund; it's the third-largest actively managed fund in the U.S., according to Morningstar. Given the fund's exceptional record since its 2007 inception, it's notable that Ivascyn has cut its corporate exposure to 3% of his portfolio.

Flexibility can be beneficial in difficult bond markets like today's — or it can hurt. Finding a good multisector fund is thus more challenging, as the difference in returns and strategies can be vast. When interest rates are rising, bond prices fall, and bonds with the longest durations fall the most. Lately multisector funds emphasizing low-duration debt have been the best performers. (Duration measures how sensitive a bond portfolio is to changes in interest rates.)

CrossingBridge Low Duration High Income thrives in such an environment, and it has never had a down calendar year. Even in 2022, when rates soared and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index fell 13% and the average multisector bond fund lost 10%, the CrossingBridge fund was up 1%. Managers David Sherman and Kirk Whitney keep the fund's duration between 0.75 and two years. It's up 2.5% this year and rose 0.5% during the volatile third quarter, when the average multisector fund fell 2.2% and the Agg index lost 3.5%.

While CrossingBridge isn't particularly flexible about duration, it is with bond sectors. "We're able to find opportunities across high yield, investment grade, and corporate credit, leveraged loans — even in premerger SPAC [special purpose acquisition company] securities," says Whitney.

Right now he likes Nordic bonds overseas, which have higher yields and better covenant debt protections than equivalent U.S. ones. He points to PolarDC Group, which owns Norwegian artificial-intelligence data centers. When the fund purchased Polar's 2030-maturity bonds this year, they were yielding 3.3 percentage points more than comparable Applied Digital U.S. data-center bonds.

Meanwhile, Pimco Income's long-term debt tilt has hurt the fund. The fund's 6.1-year duration, compared with the 4.2-year category average, made it one of the third quarter's worst performers, with a 3.9% decline. But Ivascyn isn't thinking short term. "More interest rate risk allows you to lock in these attractive portfolio yields for longer," he says. "Today, we can generate a yield of around 8% with the least amount of low-quality credit exposure the strategy has ever had. So, for the next three years, there's a high likelihood that this strategy will be able to generate that type of return."

It's worth understanding Ivascyn's long-term focus, especially since his fund's immense size makes it harder to maneuver between bond types such as nonagency mortgage debt, according to Morningstar analyst Eric Jacobson. Though Ivascyn disputes this claim, it would be nearly impossible for Pimco Income to invest meaningfully in the specialized short-term debt of CrossingBridge's boutique fund.

Yet size has benefits, too. "The biggest dominant players in the market have the ability to drive deals, get covenants, do things that aren't typical late-cycle behaviors," says Gregory Peters, co-chief investment officer of PGIM Credit. "Historically, what you've seen at the end of a credit cycle is you take whatever is given to you because there's such froth, but today large managers are driving transactions." PGIM runs more than $1 trillion in bonds, so it has the heft to dictate terms from bond issuers.

Peters co-manages two excellent multisector funds Morningstar doesn't categorize as multisector: the PGIM Short Duration Multi-Sector Bond exchange-traded fund, officially a short-term bond fund, and PGIM Absolute Return Bond, a nontraditional bond fund. Both have sector flexibility yet also a short-duration focus. The difference is that PGIM Absolute Return Bond hedges its portfolio with futures and swaps to shorten its duration. "We have the ability to move our duration to plus or minus three years," Peters says. Currently, it stands at a low 0.6 years.

Other top players, such as Nationwide Strategic Income, can hedge both credit and duration risk. Despite having a gross 54% corporate bond exposure, it falls to a net 31% one after hedges, and it has a low 1.8-year duration. It has beaten 98% of its peers in the past decade, but tends to suffer in bad markets for high-yield bonds, like 2020's first quarter.

Fidelity Strategic Income is also a strong option, albeit with a high-yield tilt. Eaton Vance has a similar focus in Eaton Vance Strategic Income and the Eaton Vance Income Opportunities ETF, which are run by the same management team.

"We focus on what we call the 'plus sectors' of fixed income — emerging markets, below-investment-grade corporate credit, and then securitized products" such as mortgage debt, Eaton manager Andrew Szczurowski says. "When you combine those three sectors, there's a lot more alpha you can add versus traditional corporates."

Right now, Szczurowski is emphasizing mortgage bonds in the Strategic Income mutual fund, with a 51% weighting. Eaton's mutual fund has a shorter duration of 4.1 years, which has enabled it to hold up better this year.
